pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5-7 (KS1/Grades K-2): minibeast habitats and micro-habitats — the specific damp, dark, sheltered or sunny places different minibeasts live (under a log, in the soil, under stones, in leaf litter, in a pond, among flowers) and WHY each creature is found there.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' — identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited; identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including MICRO-HABITATS. Working-scientifically: observing closely, identifying and classifying.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 2-LS4-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1]).
• Operational details — the key idea is MATCH between creature and place: woodlice and worms need damp/dark (they dry out in sun); pond skaters need water; butterflies need flowers. Children PREDICT what lives in a place, then check by lifting/looking. Emphasise returning creatures and habitats to how they were found (care links to the 'caring for minibeasts' topic).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): names one place a given minibeast lives (worm → soil). Tier B (age 6): predicts what will be found under a log/stone before looking and checks. Tier C (age 7): explains the match with a reason ('woodlice live under logs because it's damp and dark and they'd dry out in the sun').
bestPractices: Frame every habitat as a MATCH with a reason — 'suited to' means the place gives the creature what it needs (damp, dark, food, water), not just 'that's where it is'.
Use predict-then-check: children guess what lives under the log/stone before lifting, making their thinking visible and memorable.
Ground it in a real micro-habitat hunt and model care — lift gently, look, return the log exactly as found.
Contrast micro-habitats side by side (damp under-log vs dry sunny wall) so the difference in residents is obvious.
Draw out the consequence of a mismatch (a woodlouse in the sun dries out) to cement why creatures stay in their suited place.
keyRepresentations: A garden cross-section showing layered micro-habitats from pond to soil to canopy, each with its residents.
Predict-then-check reveal (guess → lift the log → see who's there).
A simple 'what it needs' card (damp / dark / water / flowers) linking creature to place.
commonMisconceptions: 'Animals can live anywhere' — children don't yet see that a creature needs a place that suits it; a woodlouse can't thrive on a sunny wall.
'Habitat means the whole garden/wood' — the micro-habitat idea (the specific under-log, the specific pond edge) is the new precision at KS1.
'Dark, damp places are just where dirty bugs hide' — reframing: damp/dark IS the resource these creatures need.
'If I move it somewhere nicer it'll be happier' — moving a creature out of its suited micro-habitat can harm it.
Confusing a habitat (where it lives) with what it eats — related but distinct ideas.

learn.summary: For ages 5-7 (KS1 Y2 / Grades K-2), children learn that minibeasts live in specific micro-habitats suited to their needs: woodlice, worms and slugs in damp dark places (under logs, stones, leaf litter, in soil), pond skaters and dragonfly nymphs in water, aphids, caterpillars and ladybirds on sunny leaves, and butterflies among flowers. The core idea is the MATCH between creature and place, with a reason ('damp and dark so a woodlouse won't dry out'), learned through predict-then-check hunting and by reasoning about the consequence of a mismatch. Children should also practise careful handling — lifting gently and returning logs and stones exactly as found, and never placing a creature where it could come to harm.

activities.title: Bug detective: predict then check a micro-habitat
feedback: If the right creatures appear where predicted, confirm: 'Yes — woodlice under the damp log, because they need it damp and dark.'
If a guess was wrong, name the actual residents and their need: 'Pond skaters need water to walk on, so you find them on the pond, not under the log.'
Praise careful returning of the log: 'You put the home back the way you found it — that keeps the minibeasts safe.'
activities.rationale: Predict-then-check makes children's thinking visible and memorable, and grounding it in a real micro-habitat hunt with careful handling is described as standard KS1 practice that builds the observe/identify/classify working-scientifically skills.
sourceClaims: KS1 Y2 requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and to identify and name animals in their habitats, including micro-habitats.
Micro-habitat hunts (under logs, stones, leaf litter) grounded in prediction and careful return of creatures are standard effective KS1 practice.
learnerActions: Before looking, choose a micro-habitat (under a log, under a stone, in leaf litter, in the soil, at the pond edge, among flowers) and say out loud or tap picture-guesses for what you think lives there.
Lift the log/stone gently or look closely at the pond or flowerbed to check, and compare what you found against your guess.
For each creature found, say why it is there using a 'what it needs' idea (damp / dark / water / flowers / leaves).
Put every log and stone back exactly the way you found it before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Different micro-habitats hold different creatures because each creature needs the conditions that place provides — 'suited to its habitat' means the place gives the creature what it needs, not just 'that's where it happens to be'. Damp and dark are not where 'dirty bugs hide'; they are the resource these creatures need.

activities.title: Take me home: the consequence of a mismatch
feedback: Reinforce the reason: 'Out in the sun a woodlouse would dry out — that's why it needs the damp dark under the log.'
If a child says the creature 'wants' or 'chooses' the dark, recast it: 'It survives best where it's damp — the damp keeps it from drying out.'
Stress care: 'Because moving a creature to the wrong place can hurt it, we never put one in the sun and we always return it to where it lives.'
activities.rationale: Reasoning through, or watching a modelled, consequence of a bad match helps cement why creatures stay in suited places and addresses the 'animals can live anywhere' and 'move it somewhere nicer' misconceptions. A screen simulation showing a creature struggling in the wrong place and settling in the right one can give immediate why-feedback without risking a real animal.
sourceClaims: KS1 Y2 requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and to identify and name animals in their habitats, including micro-habitats.
learnerActions: Using a screen simulation, a drawing, or spoken reasoning — never a real creature — think about a given creature in two places: a damp shaded spot versus a dry sunny patch.

Predict what would happen in each: a worm or woodlouse left on hot dry pavement would dry out and struggle, while under a damp log it settles. Never actually place a real creature in the sun to test this.
Explain in your own words why the creature needs its damp dark place to survive.
activities.intendedInsight: A creature is not free to live anywhere: moving it out of its suited micro-habitat can harm it, which is why 'suited to' matters — the need is about survival, not preference or choice.

activities.title: Compare two places side by side
feedback: Correct answer to model: 'Mostly different ones — damp-loving creatures under the log, sun-liking ones on the leaf, because each survives best in different conditions.'
If a child expects the same minibeasts everywhere, pair each creature to its conditions so place predicts creature.

If a child misreads conditions ('under a log it's dry and bright'), have them feel and observe the actual conditions under a real log, which are usually damper, darker and cooler than the open ground nearby, though this varies with weather and setting.
activities.rationale: Contrasting micro-habitats side by side makes the difference in residents obvious and is the diagnostic that separates children who think any minibeast lives anywhere from those who grasp habitat preference.
sourceClaims: Micro-habitat hunts (under logs, stones, leaf litter) grounded in prediction and careful return of creatures are standard effective KS1 practice.
learnerActions: Look at two contrasting micro-habitats at once — a damp shaded under-log spot and a dry sunny wall or leaf.
Predict whether you'd find the SAME minibeasts in both, or different ones, and say why before checking.
List who you'd expect in each: damp-loving woodlice, worms, slugs under the log; sun-liking aphids, caterpillars, ladybirds on the sunny leaf.
Match each creature to the conditions it does best in (damp, dark, sunny, leafy).
activities.intendedInsight: Because different creatures need different conditions, the place helps predict which creatures you are likely to find — where you look changes what you find.

activities.title: Garden cross-section: where everyone lives
feedback: Confirm correct placements and names zone by zone.
If a child treats the whole garden as one habitat, point to the specific under-log or pond-edge spot and its particular residents.
Prompt the reason if only the 'where' is given: 'Yes, worms in the soil — and why the soil? Because it's damp and dark.'
activities.rationale: A cross-section teaches the spatial WHERE and the precision of the micro-habitat idea well, though on its own it shows location rather than running a prediction or the consequence of a mismatch; it works best as a companion to the hunt and mismatch activities. A tap-to-reveal 'why here?' flap per zone can make the reasoning interactive.
sourceClaims: KS1 Y2 requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and to identify and name animals in their habitats, including micro-habitats.
learnerActions: Study a garden cross-section from pond to soil to leaf litter to canopy.
For each zone, name a creature that lives there and say one reason why ('why here?').
Add or draw a 'what it needs' card (damp / dark / water / flowers) linking each creature to its place.
activities.intendedInsight: A single garden contains many layered micro-habitats, each with residents suited to it — habitat means the specific place, not the whole garden.

activities.title: Sort and match creatures to habitats (check)
feedback: For a correct match, restate the reason to reinforce the 'suited to' link.
For an error, return to the conditions: 'Pond skaters need water — which group needs water?'
Watch for habitat/food confusion; clarify that where it lives and what it eats are related but different.
activities.rationale: A matching and sorting check can assess the creature–place pairing cleanly as a companion to active exploration; note it mainly confirms recognition of known pairings and does not by itself elicit independent prediction or explanation.
sourceClaims: KS1 Y2 requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and to identify and name animals in their habitats, including micro-habitats.
learnerActions: Sort a set of minibeast cards into micro-habitats: pond / soil / under-log / sunny leaf; some creatures (like worms or slugs) can fit more than one damp place, so say why you chose.
Match each creature to its habitat.
Answer 'why do woodlice hide under logs?' choosing or saying the reason (damp and dark, so they don't dry out).
activities.intendedInsight: Children can reliably link each minibeast to the conditions its habitat provides.

activities.title: Ask the minibeast (optional light intro)
feedback: Confirm the need named by the creature and connect it back to a real place to look.
Encourage the child to then go and check a real micro-habitat rather than stop at the story.
activities.rationale: A character dialogue can give a charming, accessible entry point to the concept; it is best used alongside exploring and matching, so treat it as an optional introduction rather than the main learning.
learnerActions: Pose a question to a minibeast character — 'Where do you live and why?' — and listen to or read its reply ('I live under logs because it's damp and I'd dry out in the sun').
Follow up by predicting where a different creature would say it lives.
activities.intendedInsight: Each creature's home is tied to a need it can explain, offering a friendly way into the 'suited to' idea.

constraints: Always frame a habitat as a MATCH with a reason — 'suited to' means the place gives the creature what it needs (damp, dark, food, water), not merely 'that's where it is'.
Model and require care: lift gently, look, and return logs and stones exactly as found; stress that moving a creature to the 'wrong' place can harm it.
Never demonstrate a mismatch by placing a real creature in harmful conditions (e.g. a sunny patch to watch it dry out); use a screen simulation, drawing, or predicted reasoning instead.
Recast 'the creature chooses/wants the dark' as 'it survives best where it's damp' — avoid implying conscious choice.
Keep habitat (where it lives) distinct from diet (what it eats) — related but separate ideas.

Matching/sorting and cross-section tap-to-reveal activities mainly check or display pairings; they do not by themselves elicit a prediction or the felt consequence of a mismatch, so pair them with active hunting.

Screen simulations of a creature 'shrivelling' in the sun are simplified representations of real survival pressure; present them as a model and, where possible, connect to real observation of conditions.
Specific conditions (how damp or dark a particular log is) vary with weather, material and setting — have children observe and feel actual conditions rather than assume a fixed result.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all sources[].claim entries remain unverified (verified:false) and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Activity 2's 'take me home' is a screen simulation, drawing or predicted-reasoning exercise and must never direct a child to place a real creature in harmful conditions, consistent with the care constraints.

The legacy entry asserted that a static cross-section 'can't run the predict-then-check' and that the concept 'is best learned by exploring... not by dialogue'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources, so they have been softened to scoped affordances and limits.
The shrivelling consequence is a simplification; it is pedagogically reasonable for the age but is a model of a survival effect, not a measured outcome — flagged for reviewer awareness.
Source claims about NGSS, DfE and general minibeast-education practice describe curriculum requirements/standard practice, not empirical efficacy of any specific activity here.

assess.poeTask: Before lifting a shaded, damp log, ask the child to predict which minibeasts (if any) are underneath and whether they'll match those on a nearby sunny leaf — and to say WHY. Then lift the log together and compare. The reason given before looking ('nothing / the same as everywhere' versus 'damp-loving ones like woodlice and worms') is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Why do woodlice and worms hide under logs instead of sitting on a sunny path?
If a place is wet and dark, what might you find there? What about dry and sunny?
What would happen to a worm left out on a hot, dry pavement?
assess.correctAnswer: Different ones. Minibeasts that like damp, dark places — woodlice, worms, slugs — live under the log, while ones that like sun and leaves — aphids, caterpillars, ladybirds — are on the leaf. Different creatures prefer different conditions, so where you look changes what you find.

errorPatterns.pattern: The same minibeasts live everywhere — 'you'd find the same ones in both places.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair each creature to its conditions — damp/dark for woodlice, sunny leaves for aphids — so place predicts creature.
errorPatterns.distractor: You'd find the same minibeasts in both places, because they live all over the garden.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects identical creatures under the log and on the leaf, with no notion of preference.

errorPatterns.pattern: Minibeasts think about and choose where to live, like picking a house.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recast preference as where they survive best — damp keeps a woodlouse from drying out — rather than a conscious choice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the woodlouse 'decides' it wants the dark.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the conditions — 'under a log it's dry and bright.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child feel and observe the actual conditions under a log — damp, dark, cool.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a shaded log as a dry, sunny place.

responseLevels.gap: Expects the same minibeasts everywhere, with no idea of habitat preference.
responseLevels.full: Predicts by matching creature to conditions and explains the preference, transferring the reasoning to a new micro-habitat such as a pond or soil.
responseLevels.partial: Predicts different creatures in the two places but can't link the difference to conditions (damp/dark versus sunny).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You lift up a damp log in the shade, and you also look on a sunny leaf. Would you expect to find the SAME minibeasts in both places, or different ones? Why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks any minibeast lives anywhere says 'the same.' A child who grasps habitat preference predicts different creatures and ties it to the conditions.
